title: Arrays: DS (Reverse an Array)
directAnswer: Return the array in reverse order. The clean in-place answer is two pointers: one at the start, one at the end, swap them and move inward until they meet. That's O(n) time and O(1) extra space — better than building a new reversed array, which costs O(n) space.

remember.formula:
left = 0; right = n - 1
while left < right:
    swap(a[left], a[right])
    left += 1; right -= 1
rules: Loop while `left < right` — not `≤`. When they're equal it's the middle element, which stays put.
Swap in place to keep extra space at O(1); building a new array is O(n) space and usually unnecessary.
You do exactly `n/2` swaps — each pair is touched once.
In Python you can write `a[left], a[right] = a[right], a[left]` for an atomic swap with no temp variable.
Don't confuse 'reverse in place' with `reversed()`/`Collections.reverse` if the prompt asks you to implement it.
whenToUse: Reverse an array or string in place with no extra buffer
Any 'mirror the ends inward' operation (palindrome check, rotate-by-reversal)
You need O(1) extra space and random access is available
antiSignals: Data is a singly linked list → pointer relinking, not index swapping
You must keep the original and produce a separate reversed copy → allocate a new array
Reversal is only part of a rotation → reverse three segments (rotate array)
remember.takeaway: Reverse-in-place is the canonical two-pointer warm-up: start and end pointers swap and march toward each other, stopping when they meet. O(n) time, O(1) space, n/2 swaps. The same converging-pointers idea reappears in palindrome checks and array rotation.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for an in-place two-pointer swap rather than allocating a new array, and whether you get the loop boundary (left < right) and swap right.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Looping all the way to n−1 and swapping each element twice — which reverses the array and then reverses it back to the original. Or using left <= right and pointlessly swapping the middle element with itself.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the O(1)-space in-place version up front, note it's exactly n/2 swaps, and mention the language built-ins exist but you're implementing the mechanic the question is testing.

problemStatement:
Given an array `a` of `n` integers, print or return the elements in **reverse** order. If the input is `1 4 3 2`, the reversed array is `2 3 4 1`.

Implement the reversal yourself; do the work in place where possible.
constraints: The array may have a single element
Reverse in place is preferred (O(1) extra space)
understanding: Produce the same elements in opposite order. The element at index i must end up at index n−1−i. The elegant way is to swap the outermost pair, then the next pair inward, and so on until the two pointers meet in the middle.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I reverse in place or return a new array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In place is preferred for O(1) space. If the caller needs the original preserved, build a copy instead.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I use the language's built-in reverse?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In real code yes, but this question is testing the mechanic — implement the two-pointer swap to show you know it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about an array with one element?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It's already reversed; the loop body never runs because left < right is false immediately.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are duplicates or order of equal values a concern?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — reversal preserves multiplicity and simply mirrors positions.

examples.explanation: Single element — already reversed, no swaps performed.

approaches.name: Baseline — Build a New Reversed Array
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it as the obvious approach, then note it wastes O(n) space when an in-place swap is available.
hints: The simplest idea: allocate a fresh array and copy elements from the end of the source to the front of the destination.
Where does a[i] land in the new array? At index n−1−i.
This is correct and O(n) time — but how much extra memory does it use, and can you avoid it?
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to copy n elements is O(n) time, but the second array costs O(n) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Allocate a new array of the same length and fill it by reading the source from the back.

**Why it's the natural first idea.** 'Reverse' reads as 'produce a new sequence in opposite order', so copying source index `i` to destination index `n−1−i` is a direct translation. It's easy to get right and easy to reason about.

**Why we usually don't ship it.** It allocates a whole second array — `O(n)` extra memory — to do something that can be done by rearranging the original. When the prompt allows mutation, that allocation is pure waste. The only time you'd keep it is when the caller must retain the original array unchanged.

**The pivot to in-place.** Reversing only ever *swaps* the element at `i` with the one at `n−1−i`. Each element has exactly one partner, and once both have been swapped you never touch them again. So you can do the whole thing by swapping pairs in the original array — no second buffer.
approaches.insight: Reversal is a set of independent pairwise swaps (i with n−1−i). Recognizing that each element has a single mirror partner is what lets you drop the extra array and swap in place.

dryRun.intro: Copy from the back of the source into a fresh array.

java.explanation: Element at i in the result is element at n−1−i in the source — the mirror index.
A separate array; the original a is untouched.

python.explanation: Mirror-index copy into a fresh list.
O(n) extra space is the cost of not mutating the input.

diagrams.caption: Source read back-to-front into a new array.

pitfalls: Using O(n) extra space when in-place is allowed.
Off-by-one on the mirror index (n−1−i, not n−i).
Mutating the source while also reading it if you tried to reverse 'in place' with this copy pattern.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop doesn't run; returns an empty array.

approaches.name: Two Pointers — In-Place Swap (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want: swap from both ends inward, O(1) extra space.
hints: Place one pointer at the start and one at the end. What single operation makes both ends correct at once?
Swap a[left] and a[right], then move left forward and right backward.
When should the loop stop? Think about what happens when the pointers meet or cross.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The loop runs n/2 times, each doing a constant-cost swap → O(n) time. No auxiliary array → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Use two indices, `left` starting at `0` and `right` at `n−1`, swap the elements they point to, then step both toward the center.

**Why swapping fixes two cells per step.** A reversal sends index `i` to `n−1−i`. Swapping `a[left]` with `a[right]` places *both* of those elements in their final positions simultaneously, so you only need `n/2` iterations instead of `n` moves.

**Why the loop condition is `left < right`.** When `left == right` you're at the exact middle of an odd-length array — that single element is already where it belongs, so swapping it with itself is a no-op you should skip. Using `<=` does that pointless self-swap; using `<` stops cleanly. When `left > right` the two halves have fully crossed and every pair is done.

**Why it's O(1) space.** Everything happens inside the original array; the only extra storage is the two index variables (and a temp in Java, or none in Python's tuple swap). Compared to the new-array approach, you've traded `O(n)` memory for nothing — same time, less space.

**Why this generalizes.** The converging-pointers mechanic is the backbone of palindrome checks (compare instead of swap) and the reverse-three-segments trick for array rotation. Mastering it here pays off broadly.
approaches.insight: One swap settles two elements, so reversal needs only n/2 operations. The `left < right` stop condition is the small detail that separates a correct reversal from one that either self-swaps the middle or, worse, reverses twice back to the start.

dryRun.intro: Swap ends, then step inward; stop when left and right cross.

code.python:
def reverse_array(a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    left, right = 0, len(a) - 1
    while left < right:
        a[left], a[right] = a[right], a[left]
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    return a

java.explanation: Strict < skips the middle element of odd-length arrays and stops when the halves cross.
A temp is needed in Java to swap two values without losing one.
March both pointers toward the center after each swap.

python.explanation: Tuple unpacking swaps atomically — no temp variable required.
Stop the moment the pointers meet or cross.

edgeCases.behavior: Middle element is left untouched because left < right becomes false there.
left < right is false immediately; no swap.

pitfalls: Using left <= right and self-swapping the middle element.
Looping left over the whole array and swapping a[i] with a[n−1−i] for all i — reverses, then reverses back to the original.
Forgetting the temp in Java and overwriting one value before reading it.

commonMistakes: Iterating the full length and swapping each pair twice, returning the original array.
Allocating a new array when in-place reversal is allowed.
Using left <= right and pointlessly swapping the middle element with itself.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Double reversal
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Looping i over all n indices and swapping a[i] with a[n−1−i] swaps every pair twice — the array ends up unchanged.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overwriting without a temp (Java)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Assigning a[left] = a[right] before saving a[left] loses the left value, so the swap corrupts the array.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Self-swapping the middle
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With left <= right, when the pointers meet on the center element you swap it with itself — harmless but signals an off boundary.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while left <= right:
    a[left], a[right] = a[right], a[left]
    left += 1
    right -= 1
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while left < right:
    a[left], a[right] = a[right], a[left]
    left += 1
    right -= 1
